**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

When someone asks what a book was about, it is easy to say "it was good" and get stuck. This week you learn a way to tell it back that always works.

1. Read **Three Parts of Every Story**.
2. Learn the words in **Story Words**, then win the **Crossword** and the **Matching** game.
3. Keep the **Retell It in Three Parts** chart where you can see it.
4. Sort the cards in **Beginning, Middle, or End?**
5. Use the **Retelling Frames** out loud with a partner before you write anything.
6. Take **Story Check**.
7. Lock it in with **Remember the Three Parts**.
8. Peek at **Story Questions Kids Ask** if something is bugging you.
9. Finish with **Design: A Retelling Card for a Reading Buddy** — make something a younger kid can really use.

Your job this week: retell one book out loud to somebody at home, in order, without skipping the middle. 📚

from:
## Three Parts of Every Story

Every **story** has three parts. Once you know them, you can tell any book back to somebody.

The **beginning** tells you who and where. You meet the **character**, and you find out the **setting** — the place and the time.

The **middle** is where the trouble starts. Something goes wrong. That trouble is the **problem**. The character tries to fix it, and the first try often flops.

The **end** is where the trouble gets fixed at last. That fix is the **solution**. Then things go quiet again.

Here is a short one. Ada gets a new puppy. The puppy chews her shoe, then her hat, then her library book. Ada hides them all, but the puppy keeps finding them. So Ada gives the puppy a rope toy of its own. Now the puppy chews the rope, and the shoes are safe.

Can you hear the three parts? The puppy arrives. The chewing goes on and on. The rope toy fixes it.

Now **retell** it. Say the beginning, then the middle, then the end. Keep that **order**. If you tell the end first, nobody knows why the rope toy matters.

One more trick. Listen for the word "but." Stories turn at a but. Ada loved her puppy, but it chewed her things. That little word is the door into the middle.
to:
## Retell a Story in Three Parts

A **story** tells about people, animals or other **characters** and what they do. To **retell**, tell the key events in your own words.

The **beginning** often tells who is there. It may show the **setting**: where and when the story takes place. In the **middle**, more things happen. A **problem** may lead someone to try a new plan. The **end** shows how the story finishes. Some stories have a **solution**. Others leave a question open.

Here is a made-up story. Ada gets a puppy. It chews her shoe, hat and library book. She hides her things. The puppy finds them. Then Ada gives it a rope toy. It chews the toy, and her shoes are safe.

First, the puppy arrives. Next, it chews things. Ada's first plan does not work. At the end, the toy helps. This is a story, not advice on how to train a real puppy.

Keep the events in **order** so others can follow them. You may speak, write, point to pictures or use your talk device. Check the story if you forget.

The word but can show a change: Ada liked her puppy, but it chewed her things. Look at what happens. A story need not use but to show a problem.

from: Lots of good books do. Pick the biggest one, the trouble the whole book is really about, and retell that. You can mention a smaller one after, if there is time.

from: No. Reading out loud uses the author's words. Retelling uses yours. That is why it is harder, and also why your teacher can tell whether you understood it.
to: Reading aloud uses the words on the page. A retell uses your own words. You can also use pictures or a talk device.

from: Long enough that someone who has not read the book could follow it. Three good sentences often beat twenty rushed ones. If your listener looks confused, you skipped the middle.
to: Tell enough for someone to follow the key events. Ask what part they want you to explain.

from: Go back and look for the word but, or for the moment things went wrong. That is almost always where the middle starts. Then ask yourself what the character tried.
to: Go back to the story. Look at the pictures. What happened after the start and before the end?

from: Usually, yes. A story about your own day can have a beginning, something that went wrong, and how it worked out. That is why the three parts help you tell about real things too.
to: You can use a start, middle and end to tell about your day. A true story need not have a problem.

from: You can, and grown-up writers sometimes do it on purpose. But it is a hard trick. Learn to tell it in order first, and save the flashy way for when the plain way is easy.
